name: GO Classes CS Test Series 2026 | Compiler Design | Subject Wise Test 1

question.text:
Consider the following grammar:
$S \rightarrow A a|b A c| B c \mid b B a$
$A \rightarrow d$
$B \rightarrow d$

Which of the following statements correctly describes about the properties of this  grammar?

 

  1. The grammar is both $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ and $\operatorname{LALR}(1)$.
  2. The grammar is $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ but not $\operatorname{LALR}(1)$.
  3. The grammar is neither $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ nor $\operatorname{LALR}(1)$.
  4. The grammar is $\operatorname{SLR}(1)$ grammar.

For a statement $\text{S}$ in a program, in the context of liveness analysis, the following sets are defined:

  • $\text{USE(S) :}$ the set of variables used in $\text{S}$
  • $\text{IN(S) :}$ the set of variables that are live at the entry of $\text{S}$
  • $\text{OUT(S) :}$ the set of variables that are live at the exit of $\text{S}$

Consider the following control flow graph of a program :


Which of the following is true?

  1. $\textsf{out[4] = {}}$
  2. $\textsf{in[4] = {y}}$
  3. $\textsf{in[1] = {x, y}}$
  4. $\textsf{out[2] = {y}}$

Consider the following grammar.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{X}::=\textbf { a } \mathbf{Y} \mid \mathbf{Z} \\
&\mathbf{Y}::=\textbf { a } \mid \textbf {c} \\
&\mathbf{Z}::=\textbf { b } \mathbf{Y}
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following is true for this grammar?

  1. it is $\text{LL1}$ but Not $\text{LR1}$.
  2. It is $\text{LR1}$ but Not $\text{LL1}$.
  3. It is both $\text{LL1}$ and $\text{LR1}$.
  4. It is neither $\text{LL1}$, nor $\text{LR1}$.

Consider the $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ automaton for some grammar, and assume the automaton is in the following state containing the items:

        1. $S \rightarrow S a \cdot b$

        2. $B \rightarrow a \cdot$

What must be TRUE about the stack of the $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ parser?

  1. The top of the stack must be 'a'.
  2. The top of the stack must be 'Sa' (a is on top).
  3. The top of the stack must contain 'b'.
  4. This state has Shift-Reduce conflict.

Consider the following $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ items of some unknown grammar. What can we infer about these LR(0) items?

1. $A \rightarrow B c \cdot$

2. $B \rightarrow d e \cdot$

3. $C \rightarrow f \cdot B$

  1. Item 1 and Item 2 could be part of the same $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ automaton state.
  2. Item 1 and Item 3 could be part of the same $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ automaton state.
  3.  Item 2 and Item 3 could never be part of the same $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ automaton state.
  4.  Items 1, 2, and 3 must belong to different $\operatorname{LR}(0)$ automaton states.

Consider the following grammar, where $\{a, b, c\}$ are terminal symbols:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \rightarrow a X a b \mid Y \\
& X \rightarrow b Y a \mid \varepsilon\\
& Y \rightarrow S c
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose an $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ parser starts parsing the string: abaabccaab.

What would be the content of the stack immediately before shifting the first ' c ' from the left?

  1. $abaXab$
  2. $a b S$
  3. $abSc$
  4. abY

Expressions in a certain language can be described by a grammar as follows:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& <\text { expression }>::=<\text { term }>\mid<\text { expression }>op_1<\text { term }> \\
& \left.<\text { term }>::=<\text { item }>\mid<\text { term }>op_2<\text { item }\right\rangle \\
& <\text { item }>:::=<\text { variable }>\mid<\text { number }\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$
This syntax is most appropriate when the order of evaluation is

  1. from left to right always
  2. from left to right, but $o p_1$ takes precedence over $o p_2$
  3. from left to right, but $o p_2$ takes precedence over $o p_1$
  4. in any order, but $o p_1$ takes precedence over $o p_2$

Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

  1. If a given grammar is $\text{LR(1)}$ it is also $\text{LR(0)}.$
  2. If a given grammar is $\text{LL(1)}$ it is also $\text{SLR(1)}.$
  3. If a given grammar is $\text{LR(1)}$ it is also $\text{LALR(1)}.$
  4. It is possible for a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$ but not $\text{LR(1)}.$

1. X = 2; 
2. Y = 10; 
3. Y = X * Y; 
4. A = Y * X - 2 * Y; 
5. B = X / 2 + Y; 
6. Z = 10; 
7. if (B < Z) goto 12 
8. D = Y - Z * 3; 
9. Q = Y - 8; 
10. Z = Z - Q; 
11. goto 7; 
12. X = X + Y; 
13. if (X < Z*100) goto 4; 
14. Y = D; 
15. Halt;


Identify the basic blocks and draw the CFG(control flow graph) for the code above.  Let the number of basics blocks(nodes) be $\text{M}$ and edges be $\text{N}$ then $\text{M + N}$ is? ( Do Not count/include the special entry and exit nodes in the CFG )

Consider the grammar $\mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sa} \mid \mathrm{b}$

Which of the following is/are viable prefixes?

  1. $\text{S}$
  2. $\mathrm{Sa}$
  3. $\text{b}$
  4. $\text{a}$

Consider the following grammar in which $ ext{S}$ is the start non-terminal and in which the productions for the non-terminals $ ext{A, B}$ and $ ext{C}$ are not shown. There are no other productions for $ ext{S}$.
$$
egin{aligned}
& ext{S} ightarrow  ext{A B} \mid ext{A C} \
& ext{A} ightarrow \cdots \
& ext{B} ightarrow \cdots \
& ext{C} ightarrow \cdots
\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT about the entries in row corresponding to $ ext{S}$ in $ ext{LL(1)}$ parsing table ? 
 

  1. If $\operatorname{First(A)} eq\{\varepsilon\}$ then row corresponding to $ ext{S}$ always have multiple entries
  2. If $\operatorname{First(A)}=\{\varepsilon\}, \varepsilon otin \operatorname{First}(B)$ and $\varepsilon otin \operatorname{First(C)}$ then row corresponding to $ ext{S}$ will have single entry if and only if $ ext{First(B)} \cap \operatorname{First(C)}=\varnothing$
  3. If $\operatorname{First(A)}=\{\varepsilon\}, \varepsilon \in \operatorname{First(B)}$ and $\varepsilon \in \operatorname{First(C)}$ then row corresponding to $ ext{S}$ always have multiple entries
  4. If $\varepsilon \in \operatorname{First(A)}$ then row corresponding to $ ext{S}$ always have multiple entries

Consider the $\mathrm{LL}(1)$ attribute grammar given below:


$\langle\mathrm{E}\rangle \quad \rightarrow \quad\langle\mathrm{T}\rangle \quad\langle\mathrm{TT}\rangle \quad\quad$ $\text{TT.st}$ $:=\mathrm{T} . \mathrm{val} ;$ E.val $:=$ TT.val

$\langle\mathrm{T}\rangle \quad\rightarrow \quad\text{unsigned_int}\quad $ $\text{T.val}= \text{unsigned_int.val}$

$\langle\mathrm{TT_1}\rangle\rightarrow \textbf {+}\quad\langle\mathrm{T}\rangle \quad\langle\mathrm{TT_2}\rangle \quad$ $\mathrm{TT_2 .st} := \mathrm{TT_1}.\text{st + T.val;}$ $\mathrm{TT_1 .val} := \mathrm{TT_2}.\text{val}$

$\langle\mathrm{TT}\rangle\rightarrow \quad\epsilon\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad$$\text{TT.val := TT.st}$

Which of the following attributes are synthesized or inherited?

  1. E.val is synthesized; T.val is inherited.
  2. T.val is synthesized; TT.val is inherited.
  3. Both E.val and T.val are synthesized; TT.st is inherited.
  4. TT.val is synthesized; T.val is inherited.

Consider the grammar: $S \rightarrow 0$ S $1 \mid 01$. Given the input string $000111$, which of the following sequences of actions correctly represents the bottom-up parse using shift and reduce operations?

  1.  Shift, Shift, Shift, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 01$, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Accept
  2.  Shift, Shift, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 01$, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Accept
  3.  Shift, Shift, Shift, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 01$, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Accept
  4.  Shift, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 01$, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Shift, Reduce $S \rightarrow 0 S 1$, Accept

Consider the following grammar and its semantic rules:

1. $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{LM}$

$\quad\bullet$ L.i := f1(A.i)

$\quad\bullet$ M.i := f2(L.s)

$\quad\bullet$ A.s := f3(M.s)


2. $\mathrm{A \rightarrow QR}$

$\quad\bullet$ R.i := f4(A.i)

$\quad\bullet$ Q.i := f5(R.s)

$\quad\bullet$ A.i := f6(Q.s)

Based on the given semantic rules, determine the nature of the syntax-directed definition for the grammar:

  1.  S-attributed but not L-attributed
  2.  L-attributed but not S -attributed
  3.  Both S-attributed and L-attributed
  4.  None of the above

A context-free grammar $\mathrm{G}$ is ambiguous iff

  1. $\mathrm{G}$ is not in Chomsky normal form.
  2. some string $w \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{G})$ has at least two different derivations.
  3. some string $w \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{G})$ has at least two different parse trees.
  4. every string $w \in \mathrm{L}$ (G) has at least two different parse trees.

Consider the grammar with associated semantic actions. Each attribute of a non-terminal is either inherited or synthesized.

$\mathrm G \rightarrow \mathrm{F}$$\mathrm{G.p = F.p}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow F_1 \wedge F_2}$$\mathrm{F.p = And(F_1.p , F_2.p)}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow F_1 \land F_2}$$\mathrm{F.p = Or(F_1.p , F_2.p)}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow \neg F_1}$$\mathrm{F.p = Neg(F_1.p)}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow F_1 \implies F_2}$$\mathrm{F.p = Or(Not(F_1.p) , F_2.p)}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow(F_1)}$$\mathrm{F.p = F_1.p}$
$\mathrm{F \rightarrow id}$$\mathrm{F.p = id.lexeme}$

Determine whether each attribute in the grammar is inherited or synthesized.

  1. Both G.p and F.p are synthesized.
  2.  Both G.p and F.p are inherited.
  3.  G.p is inherited and $F . p$ is synthesized.
  4.  G. P is synthesized and $F . \mathrm{p}$ is inherited.

The grammar $S \rightarrow aSa | aa$ generates all even-length strings of $a's$. We can devise a recursive-descent parser with backtrack for this grammar. If we choose to expand using the production $S \rightarrow aa$ first, we will only recognize the string "$aa$". Therefore, any reasonable recursive-descent parser will try $S \rightarrow aSa$ first.

Which of the following strings will be recognized by this parser?

  1. aa (2 a's)
  2. aaaa (4 a's)
  3. aaaaaa (6 a's)
  4. aaaaaaaa ( 8 a's)

2. Underscore characters (_) may appear in the middle of identifiers but not at the

In the context of a shift-reduce parser, given the stack content "AcBd," where A and B are non-terminals and $c$ and $d$ are terminals, which of the following could represent possible viable prefixes for the parser?

  1.  Ac
  2.  Bd
  3.  AcB
  4.  d

$\operatorname{tail}(x)=$ all of $x$ except the first character. ( $=\Lambda$ if $x$ has $<2$ characters.)

$join (x, y)=$ sequence that is the concatenation of $x$ and $y$.
For example, if $x={ }^{\prime} a b c^{\prime}$, then

$\Lambda$ is the null string.

Which of the following reverses the order of characters in a string of two or more characters if reverse $(x)=x$, where $x$ is a string with a single character?

  1. reverse $(x)=\operatorname{join}($ reverse $(\operatorname{tail}(x))$, head $(x))$
  2. reverse $(x)=\operatorname{join}(\operatorname{tail}(\operatorname{reverse}(x))$, $\operatorname{head}(x))$
  3. $reverse (x)= join ( tail (x), head (x))$
  4. reverse $(x)=\operatorname{reverse( join}\; (\operatorname{head}(x)$, $\operatorname{tail}(x)))$

If the expression $((2+3) \ast 4+5 \ast(6+7) \ast 8)+9$ is evaluated with $\ast$ having precedence over $+$, then the value obtained is the same as the value of which of the following prefix expressions?

  1. $++\ast+234 \ast \ast 5+6789$
  2. $+\ast++234 \ast \ast 5+6789$
  3. $\ast++234 \ast \ast 5++6789$
  4. $\ast+++234 \ast \ast 5+6789$

Our lexer algorithm does the following: When using regular expressions to scan an input, we resolve conflicts by taking the largest possible match at any point.

Consider the following two scanners, for each scanner, we have given tokens and their associated regular expressions (Regular expression followed by Token name in the curly braces).

$\textsf{Scanner 1:}$

a { return A ; } 
aba { return B ; } 
bab { return C ; }

$\textsf{Scanner 2:}$

b { return A ; } 
aba { return B ; } 
bab { return C ; }

For which of the (scanner, string) pair, our usual lexer algorithm, taking the largest match at every step, will fail to break the string in a way in which each piece matches one of the regular expressions.

  1. $\textsf{(Scanner 1, abab)}$
  2. $\textsf{(Scanner 1, baba)}$
  3. $\textsf{(Scanner 2, abab)}$
  4. $\textsf{(Scanner 2, baba)}$

$$
a+(b \times a)+b+c+d
$$

  1. $t_1=a+b, t_2=b \times t_1, t_3=t_2+c, t_4=t_3+d$
